title: Process Substitution: Commands as Files 🔄
description: Treat command output (or input) as a file – diff two streams, compare live data, and more.

slides.title: The Problem: Pipes Can't Go Everywhere 🚧
slides.content:
## Some Commands Expect Files

`diff` needs two files. `paste` needs file arguments. With normal pipes, you'd have to use temporary files.

**Process substitution** solves this by creating a temporary named pipe (or file descriptor) that contains the command's output.

slides.title: Syntax
slides.content:
Two forms:
- `<(command)` – provides the output of command as a file path (reading).
- `>(command)` – provides a file path that pipes to command's stdin (writing).
slides.codeSnippet:
# Compare two directory listings
diff <(ls dir1) <(ls dir2)

quizData.question: What does `diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2)` do?

options.text: It compares the output of cmd1 and cmd2 as if they were files
It runs both commands and discards output

quizData.explanation: Process substitution turns command outputs into temporary file paths that `diff` can read.

slides.title: More Uses of `<( )`
slides.content:
## Merge, Sort, Compare

- `paste <(cut -f1 file1) <(cut -f2 file2)` – combine columns from different commands.
- `comm -12 <(sort list1) <(sort list2)` – find common lines.
- `cat <(echo top) file <(echo bottom)` – concatenate command output with a real file.

quizData.question: Process substitution `<(cmd)` creates a real, permanent file on disk.
quizData.explanation: It typically creates a named pipe (FIFO) or a file descriptor in `/dev/fd/`, not a permanent file.

slides.title: The Writing Side: `>( )` ✍️
slides.content:
## Redirect Output to a Command

`>(command)` gives you a file path that sends data to the command's stdin.

```bash
tar cf >(ssh remote 'cd /backup && tar xf -') .
```
This archives current directory and sends the stream directly to a remote tar, without an intermediate file.

slides.title: ⚠️ Subshells Again
slides.content: Commands inside `>( )` run in subshells, so they can't modify the parent's variables. Use it purely for I/O.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: Use `>()` to send logs to both a file and a processing script: `exec > >(tee stdout.log) 2> >(tee stderr.log >&2)`.
